idiom_name: virtual copy function (`clone()`) returning an owning handle to the base type
implementation_notes: Declare one copy operation on the base type - conventionally `clone()`, read-only (const) and returning an owning handle to the base type (smart pointer, or the interface type itself) - and implement it in every concrete class as a copy-construction of `*this` returned as that handle. Keep the operation pure virtual at every abstract level so a forgotten override is a compile error, and pair it with a virtual destructor so the returned object can be destroyed through the base type. Decide and document shallow versus deep semantics: deep-copy every owning reference member explicitly and share only genuinely immutable state. When the type set is closed and known at compile time, a checked union/variant plus a visitor replaces the virtual hook entirely.
pitfalls: A clone that returns the base type by value slices the object: only the base sub-object is copied and all derived state is silently lost.
A clone that copies reference members shallowly leaves both objects sharing mutable state - double mutation, and double free for owning pointers.
Returning a raw pointer from clone() without a binding ownership rule leaks on every early return or exception between the call and the point where an owner takes over.

Wrong move: calling clone() from a constructor to populate a copied field -> during construction the dynamic type is the class being constructed, so the 'virtual' call binds to that level's override (or aborts on a pure-virtual call) and deeper subclasses never participate -> take the polymorphic copy at the call site after the object is fully constructed, or route creation through a factory.

Wrong move: implementing clone() as `return new Base(*this)` in a base or intermediate class that others extend -> every copy taken through the base handle has the wrong dynamic type and silently drops subclass state -> implement each override as a copy-construction of that class's own type and use a covariant return type where the language allows it.
